justification_text:
The point estimates for each horizon were primarily driven by an assumption that the underlying dynamics of the variable we are forecasting would remain relatively stable over time. In this case, the 1-day, 1-week, and 1-month point estimates (all at 292.08) reflect a base expectation that, absent major drivers of change, the value would not significantly deviate from its most recently observed or average level. This sort of assumption is common in forecasts where no dominant trend, seasonality, or external shock is apparent, and the variable being forecast is assumed to behave relatively normally over the short term.

The width of the confidence intervals, on the other hand, reflects the increasing uncertainty that naturally accumulates over longer time horizons. For the 1-day forecast, the range (289.16 to 295.00) is quite narrow because the timeframe is so short, leaving less room for unknown factors to disrupt outcomes. Over a week, uncertainty grows due to the potential for more random volatility or small shifts in the underlying factors, broadening the range to 284.24–299.92. By one month, the range becomes even wider—272.08 to 312.08—because the world has more time to change, and there is more opportunity for unexpected developments to occur.

The primary risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include unanticipated events that are not factored into the model. These might include sudden economic shocks, geopolitical events, significant policy changes, or unforeseen developments specific to the variable being forecast (e.g., a major news event or structural change in the underlying system). For the farther-out timeframes (e.g., one month), the chances of such risks are greater simply because there is more time for such uncertainty to materialize. Additionally, if the model underlying this forecast is missing key drivers of variability (e.g., seasonality or external correlations), the intervals may fail to capture the true range of possible outcomes.
